Title: Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/coordinated-disclosure-of-critical-vulnerabilities

Markdown Content:
Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our [Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window)](https://patchtheplanet.org/) initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.

For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes. [**We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/php2shell-checker)to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply.

Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory. It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.

To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a [Defender’s Window](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/) for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure.

To help more defenders use these capabilities, we’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized [Daybreak access](https://openai.com/form/enterprise-trusted-access-for-cyber/) through [Daybreak for Frontline Defenders](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-for-frontline-defenders/), focused on organizations with limited security resources protecting essential services.

As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Drawing on our experience thus far, we’re sharing a proposed approach, appropriate for the AI era, to responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software, and we’re asking the security community to help improve this framework. It brings together our models, security expertise, and maintainers to help turn findings into protection and build a response that can scale as AI capabilities advance.

## Coordinating a global response

Getting a fix into use can mean adapting it for older releases, preparing provider mitigations, and updating systems across many organizations. A repeatable process helps those teams act quickly as more vulnerabilities are discovered.

Through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare.

For some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages:

*   **Validate and fix the upstream vulnerability.** The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability.

*   **Give affected organizations time to act.** We propose a framework for considering which organizations need advance information to prepare protections, while maintainers decide whom to involve. We help with outreach, information-sharing agreements, and coordination between teams. A distributor might adapt a fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security provider might prepare detection or prevention measures, including web application firewall (WAF) rules.

*   **Coordinate with government partners to help protect critical systems.** Government agencies play an essential role in coordinating a wider response and helping security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services. In the case of PHP, we worked, in collaboration with our partners, to engage with multiple parts of the U.S. government, including the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), as well as international partners to support that effort.

*   **Prepare updates across affected products.** As the fix, guidance, and disclosure plans become stable, maintainers can involve additional distributors, hosting and service providers, response teams, and operators to prepare updates and address gaps in coverage.

*   **Once a patch is available, publish guidance and support deployment.** Public guidance helps people assess their exposure, find authoritative updates or interim mitigations, and check that a fix is running. The response continues as operators deploy updates and report where they need help.

The proposed framework considers an organization’s protective role, including protecting its own systems and customers, the time needed to act, and its ability to handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, with maintainers deciding whom to involve ahead of disclosure.

Each participant receives the information needed to carry out their protective work, from network logs with indicators of compromise to more sensitive working proof-of-concept exploits. Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability, so we weigh the risk of sharing them against the protection they enable.

Teams following this framework would work with maintainers to give defenders time to prepare and reassess the timeline if there’s active exploitation in the wild, a leak, a revealing public patch, or increased risk to users from stalled remediation.

The [Patch the Planet website⁠(opens in a new window)](https://patchtheplanet.org/) brings together public disclosures and guidance to help operators identify affected systems, find the right update, and verify that the updated software is running properly. For PHP, it points to the maintainers’ official patch and upgrade instructions and our partners’ technical research. The guidance also covers interim mitigations, when to involve a provider or expert, and backup and recovery. Interim protections can reduce risk, but we’ll make their limits and operational tradeoffs clear.

Operators can use [CISA’s guidance on prioritization and remediation⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-26-04-prioritizing-security-updates-based-risk) to assess how quickly to act based on exposure, exploitation, and potential impact. That may mean emergency patching, immediate mitigation, or a planned update, alongside forensic triage where warranted to assess whether systems have already been compromised. Priorities should be reassessed as conditions change, with a clear path to lasting remediation.

## Giving maintainers the capacity and resources to respond

Global coordination depends on the people who maintain the software. Many projects are run by small teams that review security reports alongside routine development. Those teams need help separating new issues from duplicates, assessing impact, and testing fixes across supported releases. We support that work with funding, access to capable models, and hands-on engineering help.

Powerful AI capabilities are advancing across the industry, and we expect AI to play a growing role in helping defenders find vulnerabilities, monitor systems, and respond to threats. We’re investing in models, tools, and partnerships to help defenders put those capabilities to work.

Our investments include subscriptions for all maintainers through [Codex for OSS](https://openai.com/form/codex-for-oss/) and direct sponsorship of projects such as the [Rust Foundation⁠(opens in a new window)](https://rustfoundation.org/media/rust-foundation-welcomes-openai-as-platinum-member-announces-donation-to-rust-project/) for maintainers and technical work. Each project sets its own priorities. Reusable tests and security workflows can reduce the effort needed to handle future findings. Open-source projects can [apply to Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window)](https://trailofbits.com/patch-the-planet/#apply) for hands-on support.

We’re also calibrating additional blocking classifiers for Daybreak to help reduce the potential for misuse. This involves difficult tradeoffs: safeguards intended to prevent abuse can also block legitimate security work. Broad access to capable models and effective protections against misuse are both critical. Our aim is to preserve the capabilities defenders need to find and fix vulnerabilities while limiting harmful use. We’ll continue refining that balance as capabilities advance and we learn from how these tools are used.

## Building more secure software foundations

As models become more capable, the opportunity extends beyond finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities. We want to help engineers build more secure software from the start. Improvements to a widely used component can prevent bugs or limit their impact across many products and services.

AI can help engineers understand existing code, prepare changes, and develop tests, while maintainers and security experts verify that those changes preserve the behavior users depend on. We see opportunities in several areas:

*   **Secure code from the start.** Coding models can help developers choose safer defaults, use security libraries correctly, and catch risky patterns as they write. Preventing vulnerabilities during development means fewer emergency fixes for maintainers and users.

*   **Memory-safe software.** Moving critical components to memory-safe languages can eliminate common classes of memory errors. AI can help with migrations, with tests and expert review to check behavior and compatibility.

*   **Formal verification.** Mathematical proofs can show that critical components satisfy specified security properties under stated assumptions. Applying these methods to widely used components could help rule out classes of vulnerabilities across the services and critical infrastructure that depend on them.

*   **Stronger isolation.** Systems need protection against vulnerabilities that have not yet been found or fixed. Running software that processes untrusted files, images, or media in tightly restricted sandboxes can limit the damage if it is compromised. AI can help engineers test and strengthen widely used sandboxing technologies, improving protections across many applications.

Title: OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/openai-models-google-cloud

Markdown Content:
OpenAI and [Google Cloud⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/google-cloud-brings-openai-models-to-customers) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and [Codex⁠(opens in a new window)](http://chatgpt.com/codex/) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure.

Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work.

For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads.

Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases.

Additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption.

General availability is planned in the coming weeks. Request access to OpenAI on Google Cloud [here](https://openai.com/form/openai-on-google-cloud/).

Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner.

Title: Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/scaling-ai-research-for-complex-biological-data

Markdown Content:
What if scientists could uncover new clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months? Working together, OpenAI, [PerturbAI⁠(opens in a new window)](http://perturb.ai/), and [Scripps Research⁠(opens in a new window)](http://scripps.edu/) used [thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.15.759436v1) to analyze and interpret existing experimental data from [millions of mouse brain cells⁠(opens in a new window)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/perturbai/wholebrain_crispr_atlas) in just 32 minutes. The agents connected the effects of gene disruptions with findings from scientific literature, uncovering unexpected biological connections that can help scientists understand disease and identify research directions for new treatments. The work shows how AI can help researchers explore more of what large biological experiments reveal.

Modern experiments generate far more data than scientists can thoroughly investigate. Researchers can now alter thousands of genes and measure their effects across millions of cells. But understanding what these results mean for human disease requires connecting complex experimental findings with decades of scattered scientific knowledge. This is where AI can help scientists uncover promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

> “We build cell atlases so that other scientists can make discoveries we haven’t imagined yet. AI could help more researchers explore these resources and turn unexpected observations into new questions to test.”

—Sarah Teichmann, Ph.D., Chair in Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge and founding co-chair of the Human Cell Atlas

The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined a [whole-brain CRISPR atlas⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.03.16.711480v1), a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.

The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms.

Some of these insights point to new leads for understanding brain disease. The agents identified unexpected differences in how two disease-linked genes affect brain cells differently, as well as a potential connection between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. These findings could help scientists investigate how disease develops and where future treatments might intervene.

> “Sometimes the clues are already there, scattered across different fields—we just haven’t connected them. The possible link between neuronal function and cholesterol metabolism shows how those pieces, once brought together, can give us a new way to think about disease biology.”

—Tomasz Nowakowski, Ph.D., associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF

Researchers can begin exploring these findings today. The reasoning atlas is [available⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/jinlabneurogenomics/distributed_agent), allowing scientists to compare related genes, investigate unexpected responses, and identify promising leads to pursue. New discoveries often emerge when researchers from different fields bring their expertise together and connect familiar ideas in unexpected ways. AI can significantly scale these connections by linking new data with knowledge scattered across disciplines. The opportunity goes beyond analyzing data faster. By combining AI with experimental biology, human expertise, and scientific literature, we can help scientists turn more of their data into testable ideas.

## Big experiments, unexpected clues

Some of an experiment’s most interesting clues lie outside the story scientists set out to investigate. In a dataset spanning thousands of perturbations, those clues can be easy to miss.

The agents identified an unexpected difference between Tsc1 and Tsc2, two genes that work together to control mTOR, a major regulator of cell growth, metabolism, and aging. Disrupting either gene had similar effects in several groups of neurons. But in the cerebellum, which helps coordinate movement, Tsc2 disruption altered the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication, while Tsc1 disruption produced little change.

That difference may be relevant to human disease. In people with tuberous sclerosis, abnormalities in the cerebellum are strongly linked to TSC2 mutations. While medicines that reduce mTOR activity can treat certain brain tumors and seizures, learning and behavioral difficulties associated with the disease remain challenging to address. The agents pinpointed a specific group of neurons and cellular changes worth investigating: which changes might existing medicines correct, and which might point to new treatment approaches? This gives researchers a more specific set of questions to test in the lab.

## Divide the work, deepen the reasoning

Could a single agent given the entire dataset do just as well as thousands of agents working in parallel? We tested this while keeping the model and resources fixed. As the workload grew, the single agent searched less of the literature, citing only 11 references at the largest workload, while the distributed agents cited more than 700 references. Human experts also preferred the distributed-agent interpretations.

Scientists have limited time and often focus on the strongest signals in their data. Distributed agents can help examine a wider range of responses, including subtle or unexpected ones, and connect them with relevant scientific literature. Running the agents in parallel allows many perturbations to be investigated at once. This helps scientists explore more of what an experiment contains and identify promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

_At the largest workload, distributed agents cited more than 700 references, compared with 11 for a single agent._

## Finding the next experiment worth doing

A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead in _DCTN1_, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms.

DCTN1 is involved in moving cargo inside neurons. In the whole-brain CRISPR atlas, disrupting Dctn1 increased the expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. The agents connected this observation with research suggesting that problems with cholesterol transport may cause cells to make more cholesterol. This raised a question for follow-up experiments: could DCTN1 disruption change how cholesterol is distributed within neurons, and could those changes contribute to neurodegeneration? If so, could restoring normal cholesterol distribution help protect neurons?

Human experts also considered this hypothesis novel, consequential and worth following up on. This example shows how connecting an unexpected result with existing knowledge can turn a clue into a testable idea, and potentially a new direction for treating disease.

In blinded comparisons, human experts preferred distributed-agent reports over single-agent reports 75% of the time.

Scientists remain at the center of discovery. By uncovering more promising leads, AI can help researchers decide which ideas to pursue, design experiments, and interpret results. The goal is to turn more of the information in biological experiments into knowledge that, over time, can help guide the development of better medicines.

Title: Broad access through consistent standards

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/broad-access-through-consistent-standards

Markdown Content:
Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models. We’re also updating our Usage Policies to make those requirements clearer and easier for developers to follow.

Models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build. As those capabilities grow, we’re working to keep safeguards effective and consistently applied across the services that offer our models.

## Responsibility starts with us

Before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them. As we describe in our [approach to safety and alignment](https://openai.com/safety/how-we-think-about-safety-alignment/), we combine safeguards designed to reinforce one another.

After deployment, we monitor for potential abuse and investigate concerns. To [mitigate cyber misuse](https://openai.com/index/strengthening-cyber-resilience/), for example, we train models to refuse harmful requests and use systems that look for suspicious patterns across interactions to decide how to respond. Trusted access programs provide another layer of protection and set eligibility requirements and conditions for access to our most powerful capabilities.

Some safeguards are built into the model and others depend on the systems and people around it. Both need to be effective whether people access our models directly or through a partner.

## Consistent standards across services

Developers and businesses should be able to choose where they access our models, with consistent safeguards across those services. We developed policies to align our safeguards across providers and are working with each of our partners to ensure their implementation meets or exceeds our safety standards. These policies apply whether people access our models directly through OpenAI, partners that host them, or through reseller partners.

These policies require partners that provide access to OpenAI models to maintain safeguards consistent with our own, investigate potential violations, and take appropriate action when concerns are identified. That includes coordinating on enforcement so that restrictions remain effective across services providing access to our models.

Putting this into practice means accounting for how different services work and how customers use them. Our work with customers and partners on [Private Safety Processing](https://openai.com/index/offering-zero-data-retention-for-frontier-models/) is one example of how we can develop effective safeguards while giving customers greater choice and control over their sensitive data.

## Clear policies and predictable enforcement

We’re also updating our [Usage Policies](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/), effective November 20, 2026, to clarify the rules for safe model development and sensitive uses of AI. The updated Usage Policies build on that work by requiring services that provide direct access to our models such as model routers or AI gateways to get our review and approval before offering that access.

We’ll keep explaining what’s allowed, what’s restricted, and how customers and partners can ask questions or resolve compliance concerns.

As our models become more capable, we’ll keep improving how we detect, investigate, and respond to misuse. Customers can face misuse through their end users, compromised accounts, or leaked API keys and we work with them to understand and address those problems.

We’re also working with customers to introduce SafetyIDs, which customers can provide to help us distinguish between individual end users in an investigation without OpenAI learning those users’ identities. With SafetyIDs, we can respond to potential misuse more precisely while reducing disruption to others.

We base enforcement decisions on documented conduct and risk, apply our rules consistently, and respond in proportion to the circumstances. When we restrict access, we revisit those restrictions if meaningful changes in conduct, commitments, or safeguards address the concerns behind our decision.

We want more people to benefit from AI. Clear rules and consistent safeguards should make it easier for developers and businesses to build, compete, and choose the services that work best for them.

Title: ChatGPT Ads expands to 26 new countries as over 100,000 advertisers have used the platform

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-ads-expands-26-new-countries

Markdown Content:
More than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. Ads can help people discover products and services that fit their needs, including options they might not have found otherwise.

Since we launched ads just over eight months ago, over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT. Today, we’re expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, extending availability to 89 countries worldwide. This launch builds on our recent expansions across[Europe](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-ads-expands-across-europe/) and[Southeast Asia and Taiwan](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-ads-expands-southeast-asia-taiwan/).

Advertising helps support free and low-cost access to ChatGPT for people around the world. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ads will appear only on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.

## Supporting more businesses around the world

Following our launches in Mexico and Brazil, we’re bringing ChatGPT Ads to 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru. We’re also launching in more markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.

Advertisers can access ChatGPT Ads in these countries through technology partners or self-service access through [Ads Manager⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/).

## Reach people as they explore their options

In ChatGPT, people can explain what they’re looking for, ask follow-up questions, and refine their options through conversation. Someone training for their first marathon might start by exploring meal ideas for race week, then narrow their options based on their dietary preferences and how much time they have to cook. An ad relevant to that conversation could introduce them to a grocery delivery service they hadn’t considered.

For local businesses, regional brands, and international companies, ChatGPT Ads gives businesses a way to introduce their products during these moments of consideration, when people are still evaluating their options and deciding what’s right for them.

## Guided by our ads principles

Protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT is foundational to our approach to advertising.

Guided by OpenAI’s [ads principles](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-advertising-and-expanding-access/), we keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data. Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT’s answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions—and effective for the businesses that advertise with us.

## What’s next

Our focus remains expanding access to AI while staying true to our principles.

With ChatGPT Ads now available in 89 countries, our next phase of growth will include the development of additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities. We are also continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.

As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services—and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive.

Businesses interested in advertising on ChatGPT can learn more at[ads.openai.com⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/).

Title: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/building-chatgpt-ad-stack

Markdown Content:
Traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent. A user searches for or views something online, the ads system receives those queries and page views as events, and the system looks for matching ads based on those events. Building an ads stack for ChatGPT was different: user intent develops across conversations and shifts over multiple turns of a conversation, sometimes without a fitting advertising moment. To support this new paradigm, we built a bespoke ads delivery system. This new type of ad stack is based on a custom, post-trained frontier LLM that makes tool calls for retrieval (identifying the top options), ranking (predicting user engagement), relevance (evaluating the usefulness of the ad), and running auctions for final ad selection and pricing.

Our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice. We use our post-trained LLM to orchestrate the entire ads flow, determining the right ad to surface at the right time based on both the user’s current turn and conversation history. While bootstrapping a self-improving ads system like this used to take years, ChatGPT Ads reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate [less than 200 days after launch](https://openai.com/index/expanding-access-to-ai-with-chatgpt-ads/); now, more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT since launch.

## How should ads work in agentic chat?

A conventional advertising request usually starts with a well-defined event. A user submits a search query or opens a webpage and the ads system receives a request. This type of system is fairly simple: it retrieves potential ad candidates, ranks them, runs an auction to appropriately price the opportunity, and shows the resulting ad to the user. ChatGPT does not naturally produce such a concrete moment.

In a ChatGPT conversation, people arrive with goals rather than a one-answer search query. They might be planning a trip, choosing software for their business, furnishing a home, or learning a new hobby. This doesn’t all happen in one turn of a conversation. ChatGPT often helps the user clarify what matters along the way.

As an example, our engineering team asked ChatGPT how to train for a race: A conversation begins with a general question about running. Several turns later, they ask about shoes to help train. The commercial meaning of the conversation changes as each constraint arrives—and this personalized context evolves across multiple sessions. A system that acted on the first message could retrieve the wrong intent entirely, potentially degrading the user’s experience and getting in their way.

Building our ads system required us to move beyond the request-response advertising architecture and build an ads stack from scratch to find potential economic opportunities while prioritizing user trust and value.

## Conversation memory, without influencing ChatGPT answers

Turning every message into a standalone request, like a traditional ads system, would have carried a few risks in our chat use case: 1) misreading the user goal by oversimplifying it, 2) beginning the advertising flow too soon, before the user’s real need has become clear, 3) showing ads that get in the way of the user journey instead of supporting it, and 4) inefficiently rerunning the ads flow every time the request changes, creating noise and wasting cost. Instead of building around individual events, the ads system (consisting of retrieval, ranking, and delivery) maintains a stateful session, meaning the ads session runs for the duration of an eligible turn, remembering and updating information as it evolves. ChatGPT sends the initial request context to the ads server. The ads system follows and adapts to the developing exchange rather than relying on a single flattened query.

The ads selection process runs alongside ChatGPT’s normal response generation to ensure the ads flow doesn’t influence ChatGPT’s responses. Ads are filtered and selected through a separate system consuming the conversation under its own eligibility, quality, and delivery constraints. This important architectural boundary—different services that use separate models and separate code—lets core ChatGPT servers handle generating the organic response; meanwhile, the ads system independently evaluates whether there’s an appropriate advertising opportunity and, if so, prepares a sponsored placement through a separate serving process.

_Advertising runs alongside the ChatGPT answer path._

Beyond protecting the user experience, this separation has some practical consequences. ChatGPT has no dependency on the ads system—the services are in no way intertwined and don’t share a content generation model. So if the ads serving system is unavailable or slow, ChatGPT’s organic response continues unaffected. This means the ads system can’t take down or delay the ChatGPT product. The other benefit of this separation is that it keeps the bar very high for valuable ads. Returning no ad is an ordinary, successful outcome. The system only delivers an ad if it’s clearly beneficial to users and advertisers.

## An LLM interprets conversations and calls tools

The other key architectural component in our ads stack is the post-trained LLM that interprets conversations and runs the entire ads flow in an agentic loop—making tool calls to the core functions of the ads system, from the retrieval stage to ranking to auction and, ultimately, delivery. We call this LLM the _orchestrator_.

The first part of an ads flow is understanding user intent to start the retrieval process, which is a fast and deliberately broad sourcing of potential ads to later filter through. Receiving the conversation incrementally creates a richer but more ambiguous retrieval problem because the ads system needs to distinguish current intent from stale context. The orchestrator must interpret references to earlier messages, recognize when a user is speaking hypothetically, and avoid treating every mention of a product or service as a request to buy something.

The ads orchestrator uses the available conversation and user context, iterating to find good ads and repeatedly choosing when to call which tool with the underlying goal of finding the most appropriate ad (the ad that balances high user value and high advertiser value) for that conversation and context. If the user chooses to personalize ads, the orchestrator also considers available nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations to find the best ad matches.

The ads orchestrator iteratively calls ads delivery tools to find valuable ads.

As the conversation progresses and the ads orchestrator gets more updated information, the orchestrator can run a fresh set of tool calls with the updated context to find better ads and return them to the client, which can then use these new ads if they arrive in time.

_The orchestrator is designed to balance user value and advertiser value, always putting users first._

The ads system consists of individual tools, and the orchestrator calls them iteratively to find the best ads for a conversation. At a high level, the orchestrator turns conversations into brief text summaries, which are then turned into semantic embeddings (stored meanings that are easier for an ads system to sift through), retrieves ad candidates using those semantic embeddings, filters those candidates for eligibility (based on budget, user settings, and other preliminary checks), assesses their quality and relevance, and does a final ranking to identify high value opportunities for placement at the end of a chat response. Each ad must therefore meet a high bar on eligibility and relevance in order to be eligible for placement.

### Preparing retrieval queries that capture intent

The orchestrator LLM first prepares one or more queries representing the relevant commercial intent. This can include rewriting conversation context to broaden the commercial possibilities beyond 1:1 search queries and then creating semantic representations, where the orchestrator distills a multiturn conversation into a summarized version for the retrieval system—retrieving ads from our database in a focused way.

Ad placements will be better for both users and advertisers if they only appear when there’s deep understanding of the user’s intent. Multiple queries can preserve different aspects of intent. A conversation about planning a trip, for example, might contain distinct needs related to transportation, lodging, or activities. The retrieval system can preserve these distinctions rather than compressing the entire conversation into one literal string.

As an example, let’s look at a potential conversation sequence about hiking shoes:

1.   What should I cover on a two-day trip to Yosemite?

2.   Will it be cold next week?

3.   New [insert brand] product lines?

Although the user hasn’t connected the shoe brand question to the Yosemite trip, this conversation might be represented in our ads system by two queries, such as `[shoes appropriate for hiking trip]` and `[new [brand] product lines good for travel]`. This might only be the first attempt; the orchestrator is designed to iterate on these representations until it finds ads in our inventory that are highly valuable to the user.

### Retrieving possible ads

Retrieval is the process of creating a deliberately broad pool of ad options. Candidates may come from different retrieval strategies and can later compete under the same serving constraints. We build multiple indices that optimize for different system and product constraints (for example, the index for product feed ads is designed to be aware of positive or negative product reviews as it fetches the best possible ads. This is not relevant to other ads that may not have reviews associated with them). Each index is optimized for some version of approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) search, using embeddings representing the user’s intent. This ANN search is an approximation algorithm for retrieval over large semantic indices, meaning ads are fetched very quickly, getting close to a good solution rather than looking for “the right” solution, while retaining most of the relevant candidates.

The ads system uses rewritten queries to create semantic embeddings during the ad retrieval process and produce a broad pool of ad candidates.

### Filtering ineligible candidates

The goal of filtering is to eliminate all ad candidates from consideration that don't meet the bar for placement when it comes to relevance, bids, and budget. Depending on the candidate and configuration, filtering checks can include creative and campaign availability (whether the campaign or ad-creatives are active), campaign targeting (e.g., which locales a campaign is allowed to operate in), policy restrictions (compliance requirements around what can be advertised), budget availability (whether or not a campaign still has budget available to spend), pacing (whether a campaign should be spending budget now versus another time in the day), placement compatibility (what kinds of conversations this advertisement is eligible for), and advertiser and campaign level deduplication (picking an appropriate number of ads per advertiser to ensure fair participation across businesses).

Title: Southeast Asia’s digital economy to hit $368 billion

URL Source: https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/around-the-globe/google-asia/e-conomy-sea-report-2026/

Generative AI is now an essential part of daily life for 243 million Southeast Asians. Read about how this will impact the region’s economy in our 11th e-Conomy SEA report.

* * *

Nitin Gajria

Managing Director, Southeast Asia and South Asia Frontier Markets

* * *

In Southeast Asia, generative AI has become an essential part of daily life, actively used by 243 million people (58% of the working population) and scaling four times faster than the rollout of the mobile internet. This has major implications for the region’s economy, according to the 11th edition of the annual [e-Conomy SEA report](https://economysea.withgoogle.com/)[1](https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/around-the-globe/google-asia/e-conomy-sea-report-2026/#footnote-1) . _Building the Intelligent Econom_ y, by Google, Temasek, and Bain & Company, finds that widespread AI implementation is propelling the region’s digital economy to grow 17% year-on-year (YoY) to reach $368 billion [2](https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/around-the-globe/google-asia/e-conomy-sea-report-2026/#footnote-2) in Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) in 2026. This puts it firmly on track to exceed $1 trillion by 2035. Using tokens [3](https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/around-the-globe/google-asia/e-conomy-sea-report-2026/#footnote-3) as the new benchmark for the AI economy, the report projects that growing confidence in agentic commerce will drive a 60-fold surge in regional AI usage over the next five years.

Here are the three key takeaways from this year's e-Conomy SEA 2026 report:

## 1. AI is sustaining growth in every sector.

Across the digital economy, AI is reshaping how people live, shop, and move. E-commerce ($226B GMV, +18% YoY) anchors this shift, as shoppers use multimodal discovery and in-app assistants to confidently navigate complex purchases. These personalized experiences organically drive 10% higher conversions and order volume uplifts as large as 75%.

In online travel ($59B GMV, +10% YoY), traditional search engines remain the top platform people use to plan travel, while generative AI has overtaken social media to become the second-most used tool for organizing complex itineraries.

Online media ($44B revenue, +22% YoY) is personalizing content feeds and connecting audiences with more relevant ads, yielding a 10 to 20% quality engagement uplift as commerce media becomes a $4 billion market.

Mobility and food delivery ($40B GMV, +15% YoY) saves consumers time via predictive suggestions, smarter routing, and AI-powered offerings like pooled rides, fueling healthy transactional growth.

Finally, digital financial services ($1,650B GTV, +16% YoY) help consumers with real-time fraud detection, broader credit access, and personalized financial recommendations that complement human advice, alongside Singapore’s regional leadership in digital wealth platforms.

## 2. Consumer trust will help unlock the era of agentic commerce.

Digital automation is already well established across the region, where 72% of users rely on everyday features like price tracking. This familiarity is clearing the runway for agentic commerce, with 75% expressing willingness to let AI agents autonomously compare prices and complete transactions on their behalf.

This momentum is rooted in regional optimism: people in Southeast Asia view AI as a net benefit to society, with 62% reporting greater trust in AI tools today than a year ago. Driven by proven track records (56%), rising familiarity (55%), and output accuracy (53%), this trust signals a clear runway for deeper platform integration. To feel comfortable using new agentic capabilities, users expect clarity and guardrails, including robust privacy safeguards (44%), transparent information on what AI can and cannot do (36%), and the ability to reverse agentic transactions (30%).

## **3.** Four major areas must adapt to enable AI adoption.

To support a projected 60-fold increase in regional AI usage by 2030, the region's broader digital ecosystem must systematically evolve across four critical conditions:

*   **Accelerated agentic adoption and sustainable economics:** Businesses need to move beyond using AI to answer single questions and start using it to help complete multi-step tasks from start to finish, backed by strong privacy safeguards and clear safety rules. At the same time, running AI models must keep getting more affordable and deliver clear, practical value, so businesses of all sizes can adopt the technology sustainably.
*   **Scaled physical infrastructure**: Physical expansion must rapidly keep pace with soaring compute demand. Meeting this trajectory requires a ~3x expansion in data center capacity over the next five years, with AI workloads capturing a dominant share of total infrastructure.
*   **Strict model and energy efficiency**: National frameworks, such as Singapore’s binding Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) rules under the Digital Infrastructure Bill, must guide next-generation facilities, paired with expanded clean energy access like Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS) model.
*   **Unified regional governance**: Anchoring this trajectory, the upcoming ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) in November 2026 will establish the world's first region-wide digital trade pact, providing a framework that can unlock further growth in the Southeast Asia digital economy.

Title: Bringing the Spark to Europe: Local Intelligence Powers Next Wave of Agents

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/local-ai-gtc-rtx-dgx-spark-station-sync/

Published Time: 2026-10-21T10:50:37+00:00

Markdown Content:
At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing its full lineup of local AI hardware. [RTX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/), which [launched last week](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-rtx-spark-pcs-available-today-a-new-beginning-for-windows-pcs), powers personal agents on Windows PCs; [DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/) supports developers building and scaling applications on Linux; and [DGX Station](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-station/) serves enterprise teams running frontier workloads on Linux, with a Windows version arriving in December.

Announcements include:

*   Underdog Desktop Agent now available for RTX Spark
*   DGX Spark 64GB available on Friday, Oct. 23
*   NVIDIA Sync to support eight DGX Sparks and add Model Launcher this month
*   October DGX Spark software update adds Wi-Fi Assistant and updates DGX Spark Skills
*   DGX Station improves manageability with seven new integrations
*   DGX Station for Windows launches in December with support for many manufacturing apps and agent harnesses
*   Three new open source reference workflows for robotics on DGX Station
*   NVIDIA Cloud Functions is coming in early access to DGX Station
*   Recursive Flint, a new local coding model, is now available for NVIDIA local hardware
*   Day-0 support for new Nemotron, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax and FLUX.3 AI models
*   New accelerations for llama.cpp and vLLM inference engines and a new collection of checkpoints optimized for local AI hardware.

Learn more about these local AI announcements below, and check out the demos and [sessions at GTC Berlin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-eu/gtc/session-catalog/).

## **RTX Spark Brings Personal Agents to the Windows PC**

RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — running personal agents, accelerated content creation and 1440p 100 frames-per-second gaming with up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute.

Here’s what early reviewers are saying about the platform since its October 16 release:

_“A dream machine for serious creators … ”_ — CGMag

_“Designed for the future of AI … ”_ — The Verge

_“An extremely capable, surprisingly portable and efficient machine … ”_ — PCMag

Underdog, a new desktop agent app built for fully local, private AI, is also bringing its experience to RTX Spark. Powered by its Husky model-specific inference engine, Underdog runs models entirely on device, so personal agents can get work done without user data ever leaving the PC. Underdog is available now for [download](https://underdog.ai/download).

To better enable developers and enthusiasts to build and customize local agents, many RTX Spark laptops come with an unlocked bootloader.

During the GTC keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed off how AI agents running on RTX Spark can be used to train [Hugging Face’s Microduck robot](https://pollen-robotics.com/microduck/) using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B.

ASUS, Dell Technologies, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI laptops are available today, with Acer coming soon.

Learn more about [RTX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/), and get started with the latest [RTX Spark playbooks](https://build.nvidia.com/rtx-spark).

## **DGX Spark Gives Developers Room to Build**

New [DGX Spark 64GB systems](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/local-ai-dgx-spark-64gb-sync/) — that can run models including Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B 24GB, Qwen3.8 27B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B — start rolling out from partners on Friday, Oct. 23.

When workloads require more capacity, developers can connect multiple DGX Spark systems via built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and [NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant](https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/nvidia-sync.html). This allows users to run advanced coding models like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 and GLM 5.3 Flash.

Now, DGX Spark supports clusters of up to eight units in manual configuration, enabling larger models, longer contexts, concurrent agents and distributed development. Ideal for small teams sharing a single cluster as a backend, with each developer running concurrent sessions against the same model, it delivers 1TB of unified memory — enough to run frontier-class models like GLM 5.3.

Get started with the [DGX Spark cluster playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/spark/connect-multiple-sparks).

NVIDIA Sync Model Launcher will also be available later this month. It simplifies access to local AI on a single DGX Spark or a cluster. With a few clicks, Model Launcher downloads a model and container suited to the configuration and connects the model to OpenCode. It automatically loads DGX Spark Skills for troubleshooting, device maintenance, access to official documentation and other workflow guidance.

The October DGX Spark software update brings a new Wi-Fi Assistant that lets users switch networks when DGX Spark is running in appliance mode. Plus, DGX Spark Skills provide workflow-focused guidance in troubleshooting and device maintenance directly into NVIDIA Sync via OpenCode.

DGX Spark systems are available directly from Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, HP, Lenovo, MSI and NVIDIA.

## **DGX Station Puts Frontier Intelligence at the Desk**

For larger teams, DGX Station offers 748GB of coherent memory and up to 20 petaflops of AI performance, enabling developers to run advanced models like GLM 5.3 and serve 30+ users at speeds comparable to those provided by cloud models. Adding scale, NVIDIA Sync now supports DGX Station, simplifying connections between two Linux-based systems.

New integrations with Absolute Security, Splunk by [Cisco](https://blogs.cisco.com/ai/enabling-local-ai-resilience-with-cisco-cloud-control-and-nvidia-dgx-station), [Fleet Device Managemen t](https://fleetdm.com/announcements/nvidia-gtc-2026), Microsoft Intune, Perforce Puppet, Progress Software Chef and [Tanium](https://www.tanium.com/press-releases/tanium-brings-enterprise-grade-manageability-to-nvidia-local-ai-infrastructure) let IT teams manage DGX Station systems through enterprise setup, management and conformity processes, helping accelerate approvals and reduce deployment risk while minimizing time to first token.

With the upcoming Windows-based systems, developers can build workflows that harness professional applications, run on [NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/) and operate from agents that run their large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GB300 systems — all in one machine.

[DGX Station for Windows](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-station-for-windows/), expected from system manufacturer partners in December, extends local AI into the applications and operating environment enterprises already use. Engineers can run local models and agents in Windows-native software with access to AI models, tools and agents on the same system.

DGX Station for Windows will feature support for manufacturing applications from nTop, Dassault Systèmes,Keysight Technologies, MathWorks, Rockwell Automation, Siemens, Synopsys, Unity and Altera for AI-guided design, simulation, validation and engineering automation. Users will be able to run agents using Hermes Agent, Perplexity or Aible on premises for agentic control in enterprise environments.

The same local, controlled computing model extends to robotics. DGX Station gives robotics teams dedicated compute for post-training, simulation and evaluation, shortening iteration cycles without waiting for shared infrastructure.

[NVIDIA released three open source reference workflows](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-advances-isaac-platform-for-general-purpose-robotics-with-new-reference-humanoid-frameworks-simulation-pipelines-and-data) that bring GPT-6 Astra, NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Isaac Lab-Arena and Cosmos to NVIDIA DGX Station. Developers can use them to refine GR00T 1.7 models with reinforcement learning, train dexterous manipulation skills and post-train Cosmos world models for synthetic data generation.

[NVIDIA Cloud Functions](https://developer.nvidia.com/dgx-cloud/nvcf) is coming in early access to Linux-based DGX Station. Teams can register local model endpoints in a shared catalog and access them through one OpenAI-compatible entry point.

Developers can upgrade the model behind an endpoint without changing application code, while teammates can use shared models without direct machine access. This turns a DGX Station into a locally controlled inference service for a team.

DGX Station brings local iteration to AI factory development. On the show floor at GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is previewing [DSX OS](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/dsx-os/) running on DGX Station to simulate AI factory operations before full infrastructure is available. Another demo will showcase DGX Station systems powering a local token factory for more than 30 software developers.

DGX Station systems are shipping today from ASUS, [Dell Technologies](https://www.dell.com/en-us/dt/corporate/newsroom/announcements/detailpage.press-releases~usa~2026~10~dell-technologies-and-nvidia-advance-enterprise-agentic-ai-from-the-deskside-to-data-center.htm#/filter-on/Country:en-us), GIGABYTE, HP, MSI, Supermicro and [Exxact](https://www.exxactcorp.com/Exxact-VWS-158270643-E158270643). DGX Station for Windows systems are expected to begin shipping later this year from ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, HP, MSI and Supermicro.

## **Introducing Recursive Flint — A New Local Coding Model Optimized for RTX Spark**

Today, frontier AI lab Recursive Superintelligence released [Recursive Flint](https://recursive.com/updates/introducing-recursive-flint), a local LLM built for fast, accurate coding. A 40-billion-parameter [mixture-of-experts](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/mixture-of-experts/) model with 2.5 billion active parameters, Recursive Flint delivers fast inference and performs well in agentic coding benchmarks like S WE-Bench Pro v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench verified.

Recursive Flint was built using Recursive’s Eureka Machine, a system for large-scale automated AI research. It automates the full research loop: proposes ideas, implements them, runs experiments to validate ideas and uses the results to decide what to try next — creating specialized kernels that boosted Flint’s generation speed on RTX Spark by 55% without changing the model’s weights.

Developers can [download the open weights](https://huggingface.co/RecursiveSI)on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license and run the model on RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, as well as GeForce RTX and RTX PRO GPUs. Developers can also post-train the model with [NeMo Automodel](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Automodel/blob/main/docs/model-coverage/llm/flint/flint.mdx) for supervised fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation, or LoRa, as well as [NeMo RL](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL/tree/flint-support) for group relative policy optimization.

## **New Models With Day-Zero Support**

NVIDIA is also adding day-zero model support for NVIDIA Nemotron Bolt E4B 4B, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-24B-A2B, plus the FLUX.3 Klein diffusion model.

Nemotron Bolt E4B 4GB packs natural conversation and multi-turn agentic skills into as little as 4GB of memory, powering fast local voice assistants, interactive game characters and embedded interfaces on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs, NVIDIA Jetson devices, and RTX and DGX Spark. # Google Cloud and NVIDIA Announce General Availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin Infrastructure

 Google Cloud A5X instances, accelerated by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, support European innovators with next-generation agentic and reinforcement learning infrastructure.

October 21, 2026 by[Uttara Kumar](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/uttarakumar/ "Posts by Uttara Kumar")

 Share

Share This Article

General availability of the instances is coming next month, with planned expansion of availability to Europe — bringing an integrated platform for training, inference and large-scale reinforcement learning to cloud customers.

A5X instances bring together NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, Google Cloud Virgo Network and Google Cloud’s fourth-generation advanced liquid-cooling technology for demanding agentic inference and reinforcement learning workloads at scale. Google Cloud plans to scale its Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to as many as 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites.

Ineffable Intelligence, a London-based technology company founded by AlphaGo creator David Silver, was the first customer to access A5X. Ineffable is using the platform to advance large-scale reinforcement learning and shape “superlearner” systems that learn continuously from experience.

Learning through interaction requires a continuous cycle of generating experience, evaluating outcomes and updating models, requiring infrastructure that can support the entire process at scale. [A5X](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jSsyHFW3uOs) brings Vera Rubin into Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer as an integrated system, combining compute, networking and storage to support experience-driven learning at scale.

“We’re building superlearners that continually improve through their own experience,” said David Silver, founder and CEO of Ineffable Intelligence. “That demands both substantial compute and a tight connection between generating experience and training on it, so each improvement in the agent can quickly shape its next experience. Vera Rubin’s combination of compute performance and high-bandwidth connectivity, between the Vera CPU and Rubin GPUs and between the Rubin GPUs within the rack, allow us to push the scale and ambition of our reinforcement learning research further.”

WPP, a London-based marketing and communications company, has also demonstrated its creative agent reference architecture on NVIDIA Vera Rubin-based A5X instances using NVIDIA Nemotron models and NVIDIA OpenShell, part of the [NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/openshell-reference-architecture) for safe AI agents.

The agents turn conversational requests into multistep creative workflows, such as video generation, upscaling and restyling, with human approval before execution. OpenShell provides governed sandboxes for agent execution, helping control access to sensitive brand assets and creative tools. In WPP’s initial tests, workloads that typically required a multi-node cluster ran on a single A5X instance.

As organizations deploy agentic systems, they need to protect the proprietary models and sensitive data that power these systems — even when running on infrastructure they don’t own.

Google Cloud will be among the first cloud providers to offer [NVIDIA Confidential Computing](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-model-builders-infrastructure) at rack scale on bare metal instances such as A4X Max instances powered by NVIDIA GB300 NVL72. Additionally, Google Cloud is making Confidential Computing [generally available](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/confidential-g4-gpus-are-ga) on G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, offering a flexible platform for confidential inference and fine-tuning. Customers including Vertebrae, Polaris Cloud and Confidential Core AI are using Confidential G4 for conversational privacy, verifiable agent execution and policy-governed enterprise intelligence.

To support energy-efficient deployment at scale, Google Cloud and NVIDIA are exploring [NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/european-ecosystem-builds-worlds-most-efficient-ai-factories-with-nvidia-dsx) capabilities for Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to help optimize performance per watt and expand capacity within available data-center power budgets.

[_Learn more_](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/google-cloud-infrastructure-at-nvidia-gtc-berlin-2026)_about NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Google Cloud A5X instances._

Title: NVIDIA Cloud Partners Scale Across Europe — Sovereign, Open and Built for Safe AI Agents

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/cloud-partners-europe-sovereign-safety-open-agents/

Published Time: 2026-10-21T10:30:41+00:00

Markdown Content:
Demand from AI-natives is pulling the European AI cloud ecosystem forward faster than ever. Developers need compute closer to their data, open models they can customize and serve at scale, and full-stack infrastructure that is secure by design.

[NVIDIA Cloud Partners](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gpu-cloud-computing/partners/) across Europe, the Nordics, Africa, and Central Asia are expanding regional compute capacity for model training and inference, helping developers build agentic and physical AI applications, and establishing boundaries around what agents can access and do.

Together, they’re turning Europe’s energy, data, research and industrial expertise into productive intelligence — supporting new models, applications, organizations and jobs while giving people more control over where and how they develop and deploy AI.

## **Sovereign: AI Clouds Building European AI Infrastructure**

Europe is home to world-class research, engineering talent, industrial expertise, data, the next generation of models and applications that requires large-scale computing close to where that knowledge resides. Regional AI clouds provide the infrastructure foundation on which model builders, enterprises and entire industries can grow.

As AI factories scale, power becomes a constraint which makes it critical for every watt to produce more intelligence. Nscale is using the [NVIDIA DSX Platform](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/dsx/maxlps/) to coordinate power allocation with workload requirements. In tests using NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, Nscale demonstrated that NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS enabled 37% more GPUs and nearly 50% higher aggregate inference throughput within the same provisioned power budget.

Nscale also plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for frontier-model training and production workloads to support leading model and application builders using its full-stack, vertically integrated platform with expansion across five European markets.

Crusoe is developing Spark, its liquid-cooled modular AI factories designed for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, to bring Crusoe Cloud capacity closer to users for low-latency AI inference. Crusoe Cloud serves leading model and application builders across EMEA, including Base44, Gradium, LTX and Wonderful.

Aleria,Cassava Technologies, Firebird, G42, Radiant, SWI Compute and Vultr are also developing and expanding NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure across Europe, the Nordics, Africa and Central Asia.

Regional capacity from AI clouds combines the full-stack [NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/european-ecosystem-builds-worlds-most-efficient-ai-factories-with-nvidia-dsx), including NVIDIA Vera Rubin, [NVIDIA BlueField](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/data-processing-unit/) and [NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/spectrumx/) networking, giving customers greater choice and control over where workloads and data reside while advancing sovereign computing services and economic growth.

## **Open: Models and Libraries, From Training to Inference**

Across the ecosystem, AI clouds are expanding NVIDIA-powered infrastructure and services for developers to build applications with open models and libraries. This new capacity supports model training, fine-tuning for specialized tasks and inference at scale, including applications deployed at the edge.

For production inference, Nebius has adopted NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX, using Spectrum-X Ethernet networking to integrate it with Vera Rubin NVL72 on Nebius Token Factory. The combination will bring faster token generation to latency-sensitive applications and agentic systems through the platform’s managed serverless and dedicated endpoints and familiar application programming interfaces.

For robotics and physical AI, Nebius offers a purpose-built AI cloud solution that includes its full-stack Physical AI Workbench. Robotics companies including Rhoda AI, RoboForce and Sereact are building on the platform. The company also launched three NVIDIA retail agent blueprints — covering inventory, store operations, and fine-tuning —- into early access on Nebius infrastructure.

Nebius is expanding its cloud services widely across the continent with its Physical AI Living Lab, and in Germany as a computer supplier for the Next Frontier Challenge of SPRIND, the Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation.

Baseten has developed a specialized model for code-review routing with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning used by CodeRabbit. Through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, CodeRabbit improved routing agreement from 75.8% to 80.7% while reducing estimated inference costs by 50% for the evaluated workload. The results demonstrate how AI developers can customize NVIDIA open models for specialized tasks while improving accuracy and inference efficiency.

Fireworks and Era4 are partnering to bring open models to enterprises across the U.K. and Europe. The collaboration combines Fireworks’ model training and inference platform with direct liquid-cooled capacity powered by NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs at Era4’s Chesterfield facility, supporting plans for enterprise AI solutions in financial services, insurance and life sciences.

[Mistral](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-nvidia-ai-for-industrial-engineering) is expanding its NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure to support model training, customization and inference. The expansion includes NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure planned for delivery in 2027. Trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated European data centers, Mistral Large 4 is the company’s latest frontier multimodal model, advancing capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding.

Verda plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin, continuing to promote open weight models with [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) and [NVIDIA Cosmos](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/cosmos/) already in production, and using the [NVIDIA Dynamo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/dynamo/) open source framework for inference optimization.

## **Safe: Secure Boundaries for AI Agents, From Silicon to Software**

As developers connect models to tools and business systems, they also need controls over what agents can access and do.

Announced at GTC Berlin, the [NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/openshell-reference-architecture) with support from AI cloud ecosystem partners. Built on the foundation of [NVIDIA OpenShell](https://build.nvidia.com/openshell) secure runtime software, the architecture is designed to give organizations full-stack control to deploy AI agents with clear boundaries around what agents can access and do.

NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 for model inference, [NVIDIA Vera CPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) with OpenShell for agent harnesses and tool use, and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for in-silicon enforcement. Each play a distinct role in delivering that control, working together so agents can achieve what they’re meant to do without moving beyond the boundaries people set for them.

Partners including Aleria, Baseten, Cassava, CoreWeave, Crusoe, DigitalOcean, Firebird, Fireworks, Firmus, G42, GMI Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Lightning AI,Nebius, Nscale, Radiant Verda and Vultr are supporting the OpenShell Reference Architecture to enable secure agentic deployments for their customers.

Together, European AI clouds are connecting regional infrastructure investment with the work of building and deploying AI. Expanded capacity gives builders more places to run workloads. Model and inference services help them put that capacity to use. Agent controls address what applications are allowed to do as they move into production.

Explore[NVIDIA Cloud Partners](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gpu-cloud-computing/partners/) for infrastructure and services, and the[OpenShell Reference Architecture](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/openshell-reference-architecture) for agent deployment controls.
