Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
OpenAI
disclosed a pair of safety incidents
that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code — and then lied about it.
“The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code,” Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI,
writes on X
. “When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.”
A separate incident occurred after a GPT-6.1 Sol agent suppressed automatic security alerts to OpenAI’s security team on Slack. In this case, the AI agent carried over an earlier instruction not to send any Slack messages to OpenAI’s team, using that to justify turning off the alerts.
Related
Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu
We’re running out of reasons to ignore AI safety
These incidents add to security concerns surrounding AI agents, some of which
have circumvented their testing environment’s restrictions
to hack outside companies. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI says. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.”

Title: Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI Installs a Credential Stealer and Backdoor

URL Source: https://safedep.io/litellm-pypi-compromise-credential-stealer-backdoor/

Published Time: 2026-10-21T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
• Oct 21, 2026 •6 min read

The [LiteLLM 1.107.0](https://pypi.org/project/litellm/1.107.0/) release on PyPI carries a credential stealer and a remote code execution backdoor. All seven wheels (Linux, macOS, Windows) install them as three files in `site-packages`. Both run when any Python process starts on the host, even one that never imports `litellm`. The upstream GitHub source does not contain them. PyPI has since removed the release.

Versions 1.106.2, 1.107.0rc1, and 1.107.0rc2 are clean. The companion packages that 1.107.0 pins, `litellm-proxy-extras==0.4.110` and `litellm-enterprise==0.1.78`, are also clean.

## What the attack does

Installing `litellm==1.107.0` places three files in `site-packages`. Python loads two of them each time it starts.

1.   `cook.pth` imports `cook.py`, a credential stealer. It collects SSH keys, cloud credentials, CI/CD secrets, AI tool tokens, browser passwords, and the LLM provider keys in a LiteLLM proxy database. It encrypts the data and sends it to `www.litellm[.]dev`.
2.   `sitecustomize.py` starts a background daemon. Every hour, the daemon reads a server address from a GitHub file, runs the stealer again, and downloads and runs code from that server.

## How the implant got into the release

The `pyproject.toml` in the 1.107.0 source distribution (sdist) has one extra line in the `maturin` build section:

pyproject.toml (litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz)

TOML 6 lines

The `maturin``data = "cook"` setting copies a `cook/` folder into `litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/` in the wheel. pip installs that folder into `site-packages`.

The sdist leaves out the `cook/` folder, so this line is the only visible change. No public commit in [BerriAI/litellm](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) contains `data = "cook"` or a `cook/` folder.

The wheel `RECORD` lists the three added files:

litellm-1.107.0.dist-info/RECORD

TEXT 4 lines

### The release does not match its tag

The tag `v1.107.0` points to commit [`66c8f5b`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/66c8f5b1a9cefaa7c55b758f86f4ab552f2e859e) (06:59 UTC). Its `pyproject.toml` says `version = "1.108.0"`. SafeDep compared every sdist file with the git trees by blob hash. The sdist matches a later `main` commit, [`a8113b0`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/a8113b0dd721804c752a6f1952367fb642205224) (08:50 UTC), plus five edited files and the `cook/` folder.

Four of the edited files are `Cargo.toml` files that gain a `readme = "README.md"` line. The legitimate 1.106.2 and rc2 releases have the same edit. The fifth is `pyproject.toml`, compared here with `a8113b0`:

pyproject.toml (a8113b0 → litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz)

DIFF 11 lines

The edit sets the version back to 1.107.0 and pins the companion packages to the rc2 values. As a result, a dependency diff against rc2 shows nothing unusual. The legitimate 1.106.2 sdist matches its tag commit [`49943cd`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/49943cd52ea46aacf8db2e5cb2b890d580fe9bb4) except for the `Cargo.toml``readme` lines.

### How the wheels were built

The malicious wheels match the output of the normal BerriAI release pipeline:

*   The `WHEEL` file names `maturin` 1.9.4, the same version as in the legitimate releases. The implant files have correct `RECORD` entries, which shows no edits after the build.
*   Zip timestamps show separate native builds: macOS at 11:20, Linux at 11:21, and Windows at 11:37 UTC.
*   In the Windows wheel, all 2,804 `.py` files have CRLF line endings, including the three implant files. The Linux wheel has none. A git checkout on Windows with line-ending conversion produces this pattern.

No public GitHub Actions run built or published the release. SafeDep checked all 539 runs between 09:30 and 12:30 UTC. At 11:50 UTC, about 10 minutes after the PyPI upload, `litellm-dispatcher[bot]` published the GitHub release `v1.107.0`. The same delay occurred for 1.106.2. PyPI has no provenance attestations for 1.107.0, 1.106.2, or rc2.

SafeDep assesses, with moderate to high confidence, that BerriAI’s private release pipeline built these wheels from an attacker-modified git source. The attacker could have used a compromised maintainer or bot credential, a private branch or mirror, or the reference the pipeline builds from. A stolen PyPI token used from the attacker’s own machines fits the evidence less well. Only BerriAI’s pipeline logs can confirm the cause.

## Payload 1: the credential stealer in cook.py

At startup, Python runs each line that starts with `import` in a `.pth` file in `site-packages`. `cook.pth` contains `import cook`, so the stealer runs in every Python process on the host: the application, pip, IDE language servers, and CI jobs.

`cook.py` wraps about 61 KB of Python in one layer of `exec(zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode('...')))`. The decoded code starts with this configuration:

cook.py (decoded)

PYTHON 10 lines

### What it collects

| Module | Targets |
| --- | --- |
| `sysinfo`, `netinfo` | Host name, user, operating system, IP addresses, network settings |
| `browser_pw` | Chromium saved passwords, decrypted with the profile master key (DPAPI on Windows). Firefox `logins.json` and `key4.db` |
| `browser_hist` | Browser history |
| `ssh_keys` | `~/.ssh/*` |
| `shell_hist` | `bash` and `zsh` history, PowerShell PSReadLine, `cmd` history |
| `cloud_creds` | `~/.aws/credentials` and `config`, Azure profile and tokens, `gcloud` credentials, `~/.kube/config`, `~/.docker/config.json`, `gh``hosts.yml`, `rclone.conf`, `~/.netrc` |
| `dev_secrets` | `.pem`, `.key`, `.pfx`, `.p12`, `.pk8`, `.ppk` files under `$HOME`, Composer `auth.json`, FileZilla saved servers |
| `container_creds` | Kubernetes service account token |
| `cicd_secrets` | GitLab runner `config.toml`, Jenkins `initialAdminPassword` and `master.key`, `.vault-token`, Terraform `credentials.tfrc.json`, Packer settings |
| `ai_devtools` | Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, VS Code `mcp.json`, Gemini CLI, Codex `auth.json`, Continue, Aider, Goose, `opencode`, `Qwen`, Crush, `Kiro`, Zed, Hugging Face token |
| `env_vars` | Its own environment and the environment of other processes through `/proc/<pid>/environ` |
| `db_litellm` | Reads `DATABASE_URL` and dumps the `LiteLLM_CredentialsTable` and `LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable` tables, which hold the LLM provider API keys of a LiteLLM proxy |
| `cloud_metadata` | AWS instance metadata service (IMDSv2, then v1): instance identity and role credentials |
| `gpg_keys`, `tls_privkey` | GPG keys, TLS private keys |

### How it sends the data

1.   It encrypts the JSON results with a random AES-256-CBC key, and encrypts that key with RSA-OAEP and the embedded public key.
2.   It packs the result into a tar.gz (`hdr.json`, `data.bin`, `key.bin`) and sends it in a POST request to `www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck` with the header `X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb`.
3.   After a successful upload, it writes `/tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb` so it collects only once per host. It also sets `PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE=1` to avoid a second run in the same process tree.

## Payload 2: the backdoor in sitecustomize.py

Python imports `sitecustomize` at startup, so this file also runs in every Python process.

sitecustomize.py

PYTHON 5 lines

1.   It takes an exclusive lock on `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock`, so only one daemon runs per host.
2.   It calls `fork()` and `setsid()`, sends standard input and output to `/dev/null`, and changes directory to `/` to detach from the parent process.
3.   Every hour, it:
    1.   reads `domain.txt` from the attacker’s GitHub repository and takes the first line that looks like a domain,
    2.   runs its embedded copy of the stealer, which has no once-per-host marker,
    3.   downloads `http://<domain>/codepy` and runs it with `exec()`.

The attacker can point the daemon at a new server by editing `domain.txt`. Each infected host runs whatever that server returns as `codepy`.

At 13:40 UTC, the GitHub account `letters9813` and its repository returned 404, about two hours after the release. The backdoor now finds no server address and does nothing. Hosts that ran the daemon before the deletion could have received and run second-stage code. SafeDep could not recover the server address.

## Timeline

All times are UTC on 2026-10-21.

| Time | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 06:59 | Tag `v1.107.0` commit `66c8f5b` created |
| 08:50 | Commit `a8113b0` on `main`, the base of the release source |
| 10:44 | Legitimate 1.106.2 uploaded to PyPI |
| 11:20 to 11:37 | Malicious 1.107.0 wheels built |
| 11:39 to 11:40 | 1.107.0 uploaded to PyPI (all 8 files) |
| 11:50 | `litellm-dispatcher[bot]` publishes GitHub release `v1.107.0` |
| 13:40 | Observed: 1.107.0 gone from PyPI, `letters9813` account deleted |

## Indicators of compromise

### Network

| Indicator | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `www.litellm[.]dev`, `hxxp://www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck` | Receives stolen data |
| HTTP header `X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb` | Sent with each upload |
| `raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt` | Backdoor reads its server address here (account deleted) |
| `hxxp://<domain>/codepy` | Second-stage code download |
| Requests to `169.254.169.254` from Python processes | Theft of AWS instance credentials |

### Host

| --- | --- |
| `cook.pth`, `cook.py`, `sitecustomize.py` in `site-packages` | Implant installed |
| `/tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb` | Stealer already uploaded data |
| `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock` | Backdoor daemon has run |
| Environment variable `PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE=1` | Present in infected processes |
| Detached Python daemon (parent PID 1, own session, working directory `/`) | Backdoor loop |

## Safe, secure, private

*   ### You approve

Claude Duet asks you before sensitive operations like sending messages or paying.
*   ### Safety built in

Approvals, logins, and safety checks run in your own cloud computer, so sensitive details stay private.
*   ### You see what it’s doing

You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing for you, and steer it.

## FAQ

### What is Claude Duet?

Claude Duet is a helpful, proactive agent you hand off work to through messages. Tell it what you need and it works on its own computer in the cloud, using apps you connect. It messages you when it is done or needs a decision from you. While it’s always on, it uses good judgment when it reaches out and knows what can wait.

### How does Claude Duet work?

Message Claude Duet in the app like a teammate you trust, through text or voice with no prompts or setup. Your history is in one thread. It remembers what you said before, and returns finished work like a doc, sheet, or deck for your review.

### How is Claude Duet different from Claude?

Claude Duet uses your Claude account, including memory, skills, and connectors. The Claude app waits for you to open a chat, and you work on something alongside Claude. Claude Duet comes to you. It tells you what needs your attention each morning, takes tasks you hand it by message, and reaches out when one is done or needs your approval.

### What can Claude Duet do?

Claude Duet can send a morning brief, flag what needs you in your inbox and calendar, and draft replies for you to approve. It also takes on some of the work of running a business, like finding unpaid invoices and drafting the reminders, preparing payroll for you to review, and getting contracts ready to send. It can put together a brief, deck, or dashboard too.

### Who can use Claude Duet and what does it cost?

Claude Duet is a research preview on a waitlist for Claude Pro and Max subscribers in the US. Team and Enterprise plans are not included yet.

### How does usage work for Claude Duet?

During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and uses them differently than a typical conversation. Its background checks count toward those limits. Larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.

### Where can I use Claude Duet?

Claude Duet is a standalone app for iOS and Android. On a computer, you can open it on the web at claude.ai.

### What isn’t ready yet?

Claude Duet is a research preview. It may misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent, and it can miss something that arrives between checking in with you.

Title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military

URL Source: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmreyvepnv0po

Published Time: 2026-10-21T15:41:25.512Z

Markdown Content:
9 hours ago

Christopher Giles BBC Eye investigations

Reuters

DeepMind is Google's AI company

Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use.

The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts.

Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so.

"Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity.

Supplied

Sofia Liguori resigned from Google, saying the company's push for more AI technology in the military made her feel "ashamed" to work there

In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles."

"We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."

Google is one of several tech companies that signed contracts with the US military earlier this year to deploy AI across classified military environments. The [US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy02gjq2987o), saying the Trump administration will become an "AI-first warfighting force".

But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight.

After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said.

Those values, according to [Google's AI Principles](https://ai.google/principles/), include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.

Getty Images

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said in January that the US "will become an 'AI-first' warfighting force"

The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for.

Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns.

Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future."

"Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added.

Supplied

Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch does not think current AI models are "robust enough" for military use

In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities.

The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data.

Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up.

Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation."

However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year.

Google's contract with the Pentagon, [which was signed earlier this year](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy02gjq2987o), allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control".

Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Google's AI Principles include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning with "international law and human rights"

Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations.

As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war.

"AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team.

"When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."

Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company.

"In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".

Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."

A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave – but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard."

Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]."

"Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said.

Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services".

Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.

Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch believes AI technology in warfare is not ready for the battlefield. "Current AI models are not robust enough, and I don't think they have been trained for such tasks either," he said.

_Additional reporting by Rosa Rahimi_

Local development prints the verification link in docker compose logs api , so no email provider is needed. To build from source instead of using published images, run docker compose --profile app up -d --build . A new instance has no models or machines yet. In the console, add a model provider and a model, connect this computer under Machines , and share both with your project. Sandboxes also work once your instance has a public URL . Your app, the CLI, and the dashboard all use the same REST API to launch agents, send messages, and answer approvals. Events stream back as they happen. Postgres. Every step of every agent is saved here. That record is the agent's state, so any worker can pick an agent back up after a crash or restart. Workers. Stateless processes that build the model context, call the model, and run tools. An agent only uses a worker while it's taking a turn, so one worker can serve many agents. Add workers to handle more turns at once. Machines. Each machine runs the omnarad daemon, which connects out to Omnara, so agents can run commands there without any inbound ports. Omnara also uses Redis, blob storage for attachments and tool outputs, and a memory filesystem. The architecture docs cover the details. Features Build agents Any model . Bring your own keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, LiteLLM, Ollama, or any compatible endpoint, including models you host yourself. Tools . Built-in tools for shell commands, files, web search and fetch, and asking a person a question, plus MCP servers and custom tools that run in your own systems. Skills . Package instructions and files once, attach them to any agent, and the agent loads them when it needs them. Memory . Memory stores give agents files that persist between conversations and can be shared with other agents, with read or read-write access per agent. Subagents . An agent can start subagents with a fresh context, check their progress, and send them new instructions. Each subagent is a full agent you can inspect. Run them anywhere Machines . Machines are tools the agent uses. Install the Omnara daemon on any macOS or Linux laptop, VM, or container and your agents can run commands and edit files there, with no inbound ports or SSH keys. Or use sandboxes from eleven providers (Arker, Blaxel, boxd, CreateOS, Daytona, E2B, Freestyle, Modal, Superserve, Tenki, Unikraft). An agent can use several machines at once (for example, a set of GPU servers) and move between them. If your laptop goes offline, the agent can continue in a sandbox and sync its work back with git. Durable state . Every step is saved, so agents pick up where they left off after crashes, restarts, and machine disconnects. Schedules . Cron triggers with time zones can message an existing agent, launch a new one from a profile, or start a new Slack or Discord thread . Connect them Slack, Discord, and GitHub . Walmart will soon let AI agents shop on its website for you. Next month,
the retail giant will allow you
to use an AI agent on the site, with systems in place to let you approve and review purchases and set spending limits.
The embrace of AI agents stands in stark contrast to Amazon,
which blocked Perplexity’s shopping agent
and
Meta’s Muse AI assistant
. But Walmart is opening its doors to AI shoppers — as long as they follow the retailer’s rules. It has outlined a set of terms for agents, saying that “agents must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends” and cannot change a customer’s payment method. Agents also can only access information needed to complete their task. Walmart says it will block agents that don’t follow these terms.
Your AI agent will get its own profile within your Walmart account.
Image: Walmart
Related
Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
Agents will connect to new “Agent Profiles” within Walmart. By default, Walmart will require approval for all AI agent purchases, but you can also let it shop within a certain budget, such as up to $100. You’ll also be able to review your agent’s purchases separately from your own in Agent Profiles, as well as turn off the agent at any time.
The retailer has built an “Agent Gateway,”
currently available in beta
, that connects AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that allows AI agents to plug into different services on the web. Walmart says this not only enables AI agents to shop without running into hiccups that they might encounter when navigating a browser, but also prevents them from accessing your shopping history and personal information.
“For example, if a customer tends to buy sourdough bread or a particular brand of milk, Walmart will help the agent find those usual items for the customer without sharing the customer’s broader shopping history with the agent,” Walmart says. The company will let users shop with AI agents on Sam’s Club as well.

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/att-legal

Markdown Content:
AT&T’s in-house legal department has hundreds of lawyers and legal professionals around the world. Before they can advise the business, they need to assemble facts, documents, and relevant past work, often drawing on expertise held across different teams. For David McAtee, AT&T’s Senior Executive Vice President and General Counsel, making that experience easier to access is central to how the department’s work can improve.

AT&T is working with OpenAI to build that next phase. “Our partnership with OpenAI is going to allow us to build that plumbing that powers the knowledge layer throughout the company and that all of us will draw into,” McAtee says.

The collaboration builds on LegalEdge, AT&T’s team of attorneys, legal professionals, technologists, and project managers focused on applying AI to major legal matters. The next step is to connect more of the company’s accumulated expertise to the work arriving on a lawyer’s desk.

Requests arrive from across the business, and legal teams need to respond quickly without overlooking risks. Before they can advise, they have to understand the issue, gather the relevant context and decide what needs attention first. That makes intake a critical part of protecting the business. Bill Ryan, AT&T’s Chief Compliance Officer, describes one planned initiative as an intake system with “a front door where we have natural language intake.” The system would classify and prioritize requests, connect them with relevant precedent, research, and past work, and give the responsible legal professional historical context and recommended first steps.

That would give lawyers a more informed starting point, with less time spent gathering the material they need to assess a matter. Ryan sees the opportunity in helping the department bring its judgment to more of the business’s needs.

“What most excites me about the future is expanding our ability to provide legal judgment at greater scale,” he says.

For McAtee, the principle guiding that work remains clear: “The decision making will always remain with the lawyers.” The partnership’s goal is to put better information within reach so those lawyers can spend more time applying their expertise.

Justine Calma
is a senior science reporter covering energy and the environment with more than a decade of experience. She is also the host of
Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home
, a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals.
A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.
New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.
Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new
report
from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”
In that scenario,
fine particle pollution or soot
from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006.
Smog-forming NOx
emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.
That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are
speculative
and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.
NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.
Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and
Texas has become the leading data center market
in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie
report
published in March. And in many cases, developers are
turning to less efficient gas turbine technology
in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

Are we there yet?
Read the rest of the package
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.
The sticking points
Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example,
utter a different series of yips
when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.
There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.
The progress
Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate.
Hydrophones
at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “
biologgers
” can record a bat’s every squeak.
In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to
detect vocalizations of carrion crows
and determine which bird made which call.
They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species.
That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings.
As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says.
Progress meter ............ 4
Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.

## TLDR

A remote, unauthenticated client can force an HTTP/3 server to allocate tens to thousands of times more memory than it sends. One connection is enough to OOM or pin a default-configured server. Seven of the ten implementations tested are vulnerable; several are already fixed.

QPACK compresses HTTP/3 headers to minimize traffic sent over the wire. Across the affected implementations, decoded-header limits are missing, incomplete, or applied too late. A small HEADERS frame can therefore expand into hundreds of thousands of header objects in memory. Preventing that expansion from exhausting resources requires enforcing a cumulative budget as fields are decoded and retained.

## Background

During recent research into the different QUIC stacks for our active TLS scanner, JA4Scan, I found the same class of vulnerability across multiple HTTP/3 implementations. A remote, unauthenticated client can send HTTP/3 traffic that forces the server to allocate far more memory than the encoded request occupies on the wire.

This investigation started after reading Gal Bar Nahum's [MadeYouReset](https://galbarnahum.com/made-you-reset) series on HTTP/2 request-cancellation DoS. That work got me looking at whether HTTP/3's QPACK header compression had similar amplification issues.

HTTP/3 compresses headers using QPACK, so repeated fields like `user-agent` or `content-type` can be sent as a small index instead of the full string. It uses two lookup tables: a static table, a hardcoded set of common fields defined by the specification, and a dynamic table, built up at runtime between a client and server as new headers are seen.

For example, a 71-byte header like `strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includesubdomains; preload` becomes a single byte: `0xFA`, a static-table reference to index 58.

RFC 9114 Section 4.2.2 defines how servers should limit decoded header size:

The size of a field list is calculated based on the uncompressed size of fields, including the length of the name and value in bytes plus an overhead of 32 bytes for each field.

Some implementations tested got at least one of these wrong:

1.   They check the compressed frame size, not the decoded size

2.   They decompress everything before checking

3.   They omit the 32-byte overhead from their size calculation

4.   They default to unlimited when the setting is unconfigured

5.   They never enforce the setting at all, even when it is configured

## How does it work?

The goal is to maximize the number of headers inside a single HEADERS frame. For this variant, I use unique names to create distinct entries in the receiving header map: `a` through `z`, `aa` through `zz`, then three and four char names until the encoded-size budget is filled. There are 676 possible two-letter names but we need to skip `te` as that header has special value requirements..

A 1,000,000-byte HEADERS frame holds about 160,000 unique headers this way.

What the server does with those 160,000+ headers is where it breaks.

The accordion also works in the other direction. Instead of many small headers, the dynamic table variant inserts one large entry (~4 KiB) via the encoder stream, then references it thousands of times with 1-byte indexed references. Each reference forces a fresh allocation and copy of the full entry. This is how the lsquic and Bun attacks work: each 1-byte reference materializes the full entry, a ratio of 4064:1.

## quic-go

quic-go is the Go library behind Caddy, Traefik, and cloudflared. Its HTTP/3 server limits the HEADERS _frame_ to 1 MiB (`DefaultMaxHeaderBytes`), but that limit applies to the compressed QPACK payload, not the decoded output. `DecodeFull` in `qpack/decoder.go` decompresses the entire block in one pass and returns a `[]HeaderField` slice, which is then converted into an `http.Header` map.

The `http.Header` map is a `map[string][]string`, whose keys, value slices and internal storage add overhead beyond the encoded headers. The 1,000,000-byte QPACK block decodes into 160,075 fields and retained approximately 15 MiB in the resulting request after gc, about 15 times the encoded size.

quic-go limited the compressed HEADERS frame without enforcing a corresponding decoded-header budget.

**Fix**: quic-go now sends `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE`, uses incremental QPACK decoding that checks size after each entry, and aborts with HTTP 431 on the server side.

## Cloudflare quiche

quiche had two issues rolled into one CVE.

First, `decode()` in `qpack/decoder.rs` uses `name.len() + value.len()` for size accounting, omitting the RFC-mandated 32-byte overhead per field. This lets an attacker fit up to 33x more headers than the limit intends:

With `max_field_section_size = 1 MiB`, the RFC allows ~32,000 headers (each costing at least 33 bytes). quiche's calculation allows ~1,000,000 one-byte headers to pass.

Second, quiche's HTTP/3 frame parser pre-allocates buffers based on the declared frame length before receiving the payload. An attacker declares a 16 MiB SETTINGS or GOAWAY frame, triggering immediate memory allocation, then never sends the data.

**Fix**: quiche 0.29.3 adds the 32-byte overhead and fixes frame pre-allocation.

## lsquic

lsquic's vulnerability is the deepest I found. Three issues compound:

1.   _header\_out\_dynamic\_entry_ allocates and copies per reference with no cumulative decoded-size limit

2.   _es\_max\_header\_list\_size_ defaults to 0 (unlimited) and is never passed to the QPACK decoder

3.   The 64 KiB header cap resets per HEADERS **block**, not per stream, and lsquic accepts unlimited HEADERS blocks before DATA on a single stream

Dynamic-table references produce greater amplification in this implementation:

1.   Insert one ~4 KiB entry via the encoder stream.

2.   On each request stream, send a chain of HEADERS frames, each containing 15 one-byte indexed references.

Less than 10 MiB of wire traffic and 50 connections manage to pin the resident memory at the 5 GiB cap within a second, with cgroup `memory.events` recording 900+ limit hits. The PoC defaults (10 connections, 256 MiB container) show the same effect at a smaller scale.

**Fix**: fixed in lsquic 4.9.0 (July 15, 2026), which adds `es_max_header_sets` (server default 1) to cap the decoded header sets buffered per stream and suspend HTTP/3 parsing until the application drains them.

During testing, I also observed production servers, including `www.litespeedtech.com`, advertising `QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY=4096` and `MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE=65536`.

## Bun

Bun's HTTP/3 support uses lsquic under the hood but replaces lsquic's built-in header-set callbacks (which cap at 64 KiB cumulative) with its own `us_quic_hsi_prepare/process` in `quic.c`, which check per-header size (64 KiB) but never cumulative. The `es_max_header_list_size=16384` is advertised in SETTINGS but never enforced.

Same dynamic table trick: 1 connection, 100 streams, up to 500K one-byte references per stream to a 4 KiB entry. Only 60K references per stream (5.8 MiB of wire in total) are enough to OOM-kill a 2 GiB container.

Bun has a second bug in the same function that turns the amplification into a permanent denial of service. `us_quic_hsi_prepare` tracks buffer capacity in an `unsigned int` and grows it by doubling:

Once the decoded header set passes 2 GiB, `need` exceeds 2^31 and `ncap` doubles through 2^31 to 0. From zero, `ncap *= 2` stays zero forever and `0 < need` never becomes false: an infinite loop inside `lsquic_engine_process_conns`.

**A single stream carrying ~516 KiB of wire (528,500 indexed references) leaves the server pinned at 100% CPU and it never recovers, blocking out new incoming requests.**

The missing cumulative limit is what makes the overflow reachable; lsquic's stock 64 KiB cap prevents it.

The fix for both issues is the same check (`if (h->len + space > 16 * 1024) return NULL;`)

## aioquic / mitmproxy

aioquic is the Python HTTP/3 library used by mitmproxy and hypercorn. It defines `MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` as a setting constant, parses it from the peer, stores it yet never checks it during decoding. `_decode_headers()` returns all decoded headers unconditionally.

aioquic's flow control also auto-doubles with no ceiling (`limit.value *= 2` when >50% consumed), so a single connection can deliver unlimited data.

The library itself only holds the decoded list transiently, so a minimal aioquic server that drops the headers after handling them survives, mitmproxy doesn't: it builds an `http.Request` per stream and keeps it while the stream is open.

## Why does it happen?

The harder question is who owns the limit. Decoding and storing headers can involve several components:

*   **QUIC** accounts for bytes received on the stream. It has no visibility into the header objects those bytes become.

*   **The QPACK decoder** reconstructs the fields. Depending on its API, it may enforce a decoded-size budget or leave that responsibility to its caller.

*   **The HTTP/3 layer and application** turn those fields into request objects and retain them. Their containers have their own memory costs and capacity limits.
